questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The academic level was crucial to me. I wanted to be able to combine the social and adventure-like experience of an exchange semester with great learning possibilities. NYU offers both a very high level and diverse range of courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really enjoyed my semester abroad. Both the school, the people and the city is amazing and very different from CPH. It definitely went above my expectations in all aspects.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I would say relatively easy upon arrival. However, it was very challenging to make sure that all pre-arrival requirements were met. Furthermore, my experience was that NYU set seemingly very tight deadlines, that in some cases proved to be more lenient in reality (might be due to COVID).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: My interactions with the school administration was quite limited to be honest. However, pre-arrival I had many conversations with Amy Wilson who is extremely helpful. I recommend reaching out to her if any question arises regarding the different school-related requirements.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There are loads of offers such as seminars where questions can be asked to the staff that are responsible for international students.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It wasn't very easy, I think I just got super lucky and got an apartment in East Village/Bowery. My recommendation would be to make facebook-posts in the various groups with danish people living in New York, people are very eager to help, and that is how i found the housing. The FB group is called "danskere i New York". Overall, I would recommend finding housing in the areas surrounding the campus which is at Washington Square Park. If i could pick an area knowing what I know now i would try to find something in Greenwich Village, Soho, west part of East Village or something in that vicinity. I though about expanding my search, but was very happy with west East Village and being within walking distance of the School. All of the above-mentioned areas are awesome, diverse and safe to live in.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can hinder some of the natural interactions with other students that you would otherwise have in the halls/with roommates. If you are going alone that should be part of the consideration.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The on-campus housing is quite expensive. I have no personal experience living there, but from what I have heard and seen it is quite decent. Living off-campus is equally expensive.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration proces is a bit different from what KU does, but it actually seems to work well and create a fair distribution. It's important to remember that there are multiple "bidding cycles" where you are able to change courses if necessary. I changed one course after the first class because I realized that I would rather have another course. The whole process is described in detail by NYU in the material provided, so just read through it carefully and it should be relatively straight forward.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Students are given 1000 points each that can then be distributed across the courses that you choose to prioritize. This also means that you can bid more on the courses that are important to you.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
I recommend taking a look at the link below which shows the historical clearing prices for the courses. This makes it possible to be a bit tactical in the bidding by relying on the historical data. You dont want to "waste" bidding points on courses that almost always are very cheap for example. I hope it helps.
https://www.law.nyu.edu/recordsandregistration/using-courses/clearing-prices-closed-classes

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all classes that I wanted (however not immediately - the last one I got in one of the last cycles by bidding all my leftover points).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Learn the system, and take time to read about the courses. I would also recommend reading about the class professor before choosing a course. Many professors at NYU are world-class and the professor is of course very important in how good a course actually proves to be.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not much to say here. The classes are extremely diverse, and I think all students regardless of interests would be able to fill their spots with interesting classes. The professors are experts within their respective fields and extremely competent. I was surprised at how good the programme was, even though I had high expectations.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think the level is very different depending on the course. I had a 3 courses, and all of them were very different in level ranging from clearly above KU-master-course-level to equal to that. This goes both for work-load and complexity of material. The teachers have higher expectations than at KU, and expect more independent thinking from the students than at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Teaching style is different. There are some cold calling (3 out of 4 classes for me) but not too bad. One positive from the cold calling is that almost all students are very well prepared for the classes, creating a very good and dynamic class-room environment with interesting discussions. Furthermore, you are only taught by the professor in the course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1) Contracts, 4 credits 
2) Corporate Finance, 3 credits 
3) Antitrust Law, 4 credits 
4) Graduate Lawyering, 1 credits

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all the courses I took except GL. Graduate Lawyering is just a small skills course, but not necessary.

Contracts was by far the "easiest" course I took, and was very important in creating a balance where I had a realistic chance of actually being prepared for other classes, while still experiencing the city. The professor Kieth Sharfman is both competent, very nice and understanding. It is an LLM course, so the other students are also international (LLM students and exchange students). 


Corporate Finance was extremely interesting and really furthered my understanding of the various themes within the finance world. It is not exactly a law course, but that shouldn't scare one away. The professor in CF is probably the best professor I had (Anjolein Schmeits). The final is very calculation-heavy and only a financial calculator is allowed, but the professor has sessions where you can practice for the exam issues outside regular hours. 

Lastly I took Antitrust Law. The professor Scott Hemphill was extremely competent, and brought in very interesting people to discuss different areas of Antitrust law. This course was by far the one that required the most reading and preparation, but was also very rewarding and interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't exactly unexpected, but living in Manhattan is very expensive. This goes for both food, housing, eating out, getting drinks etc.

I was surprised that takeaway was also relatively expensive except the 1 dollar slices of course.Everything was more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are many opportunities to join clubs. I played soccer on an intramural team a couple of times a week.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are all sorts of activities. All of them are available in the material that NYU provides both before and after arrival.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: COVID did have an impact on many of the non-academic activities. However, you should make use of the free gyms, and read your emails that often contain interesting activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to Cold Spring, which is an hour away from NYC and quite a popular hiking spot. It's a beautiful getaway and break from the busy city life!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had no issues with this. People are very welcoming, and the environment is very international.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs, join sports teams and attend events.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are not afraid to stand out and be who they are. It's very refreshing to see how people dress and act exactly as they would like to.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) once again it's very expensive, remember to adjust for that in scholarship applications 2) don't stress out that other students are reading more than you, follow your usual routine that works 3) remember to explore the city and take part in social activities, there is room for exam preparation later on.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Ask others, especially the local students for pre-made outlines from former students and use it as a basis for note taking. Saves time and allows for listening instead of constant typing.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in Manhattan, making friends and the inspiring academic environment

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the higher workload, especially at the start where the english legal terminology is new and slows the reading down a bit. Balancing studying with social activities and exploring the city.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
